source.title: Addition Machines, Automatic Functions and Open Problems of Floyd and Knuth

accepted.question_text: In Floyd and Knuth's integer addition-machine model, registers hold integers and the unit-cost primitive instructions include adding or subtracting register contents, comparing register contents with conditional branching, unconditional jumps, reading input, and writing output. Without treating arbitrary integer constants as primitive register operations, can an integer addition machine using only five registers compute the square x^2 of an integer input x in O(log x) operations, and can such a machine compute the integer quotient floor(y/z), for inputs where the quotient is defined, in O(log(y/z)) operations?
accepted.context_brief: five-register linear-time squaring and integer division

evidence.quote: The precise model of Floyd and Knuth [13] allows the following primitive operations which count each as 1 step: Adding or subtracting two registers
(2) Can an integer addition machine with only 5 registers compute x2 in O(log x) operations? Can it compute the quotient floor(y/z) in O(log y/z) operations?
In Open Problem (2) they asked whether the number of five registers to do squaring, integer multiplication and integer division in linear time can be obtained and the answer is affirmative.

accepted.question_text: For an integer addition machine on integer registers, given nonnegative integers x, y, and z with 0 <= x, y < z, can the machine compute x^y mod z in truly asymptotically fewer than (log y)(log z) operations, namely in o((log y)(log z)) operations? A complete resolution should determine the answer under all common definitions of multivariate little-o, because the maximum-based convention yields a negative answer while the other common conventions are not fully settled.
accepted.context_brief: sub-log-product modular exponentiation on addition machines

evidence.quote: (3) Can an integer addition machine compute xy mod z in o((log y)(log z)) operations, given 0 <= x, y < z?
Open problems (3) and (4) ask whether algorithms provided by Floyd and Knuth can be improved asymptotically
When one takes the Wikipedia definition (a) of the Little Oh Calculus, one can answer both (3) and (4) to the negative
Thus these two problems are only partially solved and would be completely solved only when they are answered for all common versions of the multivariate Oh Calculus

accepted.question_text: For an integer addition machine, given an arbitrary sequence of positive integers q_1, q_2, ..., q_m, can the machine sort the sequence in o((m + log(q_1 q_2 ... q_m)) log m) steps? A complete resolution should answer the asymptotic-improvement question for all common definitions of multivariate little-o, since the maximum-based convention gives a negative answer but alternative conventions remain only partially resolved.
accepted.context_brief: sub-bound sorting of positive integers on addition machines

evidence.quote: (4) Can an integer addition machine sort an arbitrary sequence of positive integers <q1, q2, . . . , qm> in o((m + log(q1 * q2 * . . . * qm) log m) steps?
Open Problem (4) is answered "no" when one bases the Little Oh Calculus on version (a) which is the one on Wikipedia
Thus these two problems are only partially solved and would be completely solved only when they are answered for all common versions of the multivariate Oh Calculus

accepted.question_text: Given a natural number x as input to an integer addition machine, can the machine compute and output all powers of 2 that appear in the binary representation of x in subquadratic time o((log x)^2), with the powers allowed to be output in any order? For example, when x = 13, the desired output set is {8, 4, 1}.
accepted.context_brief: outputting binary powers in subquadratic time

evidence.quote: (5) Can the powers of 2 in the binary representation of x be computed and output by an integer addition machine in o((log x)2) steps?
For example, if x = 13, the program should output the numbers 8, 4, 1 in some order.

In Open Problem (5) they asked whether one can improve the runtime of an algorithm to output all powers of two appearing in the binary representation of a natural number in subquadratic time and the answer is that it can even be done in linear time.
